kamsya-bhasma.insufficientReason: No permitted source contains a monograph, composition, elemental analysis, dose, adverse-effect report, toxicity study or clinical study of Kamsya Bhasma (also transliterated Kansya Bhasma). Searches run on 10 September 2026: PubMed and PMC for 'Kamsya bhasma', 'Kansya bhasma', 'bell metal bhasma' and bronze or copper-tin alloy Ayurvedic preparations; Liu et al. (2019), a review of the chemistry and toxicity of bhasma metals, which enumerates Suvarna (gold), Rajata (silver), Tamra (copper), Lauha (iron), Naga (lead), Yashada (zinc), Vanga (tin), Parada (mercury), Abhraka (mica) and Manahshila (arsenic) and does not mention Kamsya, Kansya, bell metal or any copper-tin alloy; Sarkar et al. (2010), a review of metal pharmacology in Ayurvedic literature, which lists mercury, gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead and zinc and likewise names no alloy; and ayush.gov.in and pharmacopoeia.gov.in for Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India and Ayurvedic Formulary of India monographs. The commonly repeated identification of Kamsya as bell metal or bronze, an approximately 4:1 copper-to-tin alloy, appears only on commercial and non-indexed sites, which this project does not permit as citations, so the metal base is not asserted here. No dose, no dose-range and no dose-limit for this preparation exists in any permitted source, in humans or in animals, so no dose field is given. Everything below is class-level evidence about bhasmas and Ayurvedic metallic preparations. None of it is a measurement of this product, and none of it should be read as establishing either that Kamsya Bhasma does contain a particular metal or that it does not.

heavyMetals.text: The metal base of Kamsya Bhasma cannot be stated from any permitted source, and no permitted source reports its elemental analysis. Liu et al. (eCAM, 2019) define bhasmas as metallic or mineral preparations subjected to repeated incineration with herbal juice or decoction and animal-based products, and enumerate the metals used: gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, zinc, tin, mercury, mica and arsenic. Neither Liu et al. nor Sarkar et al. (2010) includes Kamsya or any alloy in that enumeration, so class-level bhasma data is the only evidence available and it may not describe this preparation. Saper et al. (JAMA, 2008) analysed 193 Ayurvedic medicines bought over the internet from 37 manufacturers and found detectable lead, mercury or arsenic in 20.7% (95% CI 15.2 to 27.1), rising to 40.6% among rasa shastra products against 17.1% for non-rasa shastra (P = .007), with median lead 11.5 ug/g and median mercury 20,800 ug/g in the rasa shastra subset; the authors note as limitations possible misclassification of country of origin and of rasa shastra status, batch-to-batch variability, and that internet-purchased products may not represent those dispensed by practitioners. Mikulski et al. (2018) analysed 252 Ayurvedic samples collected during a US lead-poisoning cluster investigation, which is a sample selected for suspected contamination rather than a random market survey: lead was present in 65% (median 4.9 mg/kg, maximum 43,200 mg/kg), mercury in 38.5% (median 53.0 mg/kg, maximum 279,000 mg/kg) and arsenic in 32.5% (median 8.4 mg/kg, maximum 44,800 mg/kg); roughly 36%, 49.5% and 39.5% of the positive samples exceeded acceptable daily intake for lead, mercury and arsenic respectively; the highest arsenic content was in a bhasma, Swarna Bhasma, at 22.4 mg per pill; the authors state that no metal speciation analysis was performed, so the chemical forms present were not determined. Bhalla and Pannu (2022) analysed 42 of 43 Ayurvedic preparations collected in Chandigarh by ICP-MS: mercury exceeded the 1 ug/g permissible limit in 29, zinc exceeded 50 ug/g in 35, arsenic exceeded 10 ug/g in 6 and lead exceeded 10 ug/g in 2, cadmium was not detected in any sample, all 42 contained iron and zinc, 41 contained copper, 73.8% exceeded the limit for mercury, arsenic or lead, and only 27.9% (12 of 43) declared heavy metals on the label; the authors state that this is a single-centre observation, which limits generalisability, and that the study did not identify the source of the metals. Liu et al. also report that the toxicity of copper-based Tamra Bhasma is markedly reduced by shodhana and argue that chemical form rather than total metal content governs toxicity; the same review states that reported cases of metal poisoning from these preparations are increasing and that pharmacovigilance is needed, so processing is not evidence of safety for any specific product. The FDA states that some Ayurvedic products include heavy metals such as lead, mercury, arsenic, iron and zinc, that there are no FDA-approved Ayurvedic products, and that chronic exposure to heavy metals leads to accumulation in the body and harmful effects. NCCIH reports that about one in four of the supplements tested had high levels of lead and almost half had high levels of mercury. Because Bhalla and Pannu found undeclared metals in the great majority of products they tested, an unanalysed bhasma cannot be assumed to be metal-free.

adverseEffects.effect: Effects of chronic heavy-metal accumulation named by FDA: high blood pressure, kidney injury, fatigue, gastrointestinal symptoms including abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, and nervous-system symptoms including burning or tingling in the fingers and/or toes, weakness in the limbs, dizziness, agitation and confusion
adverseEffects.frequency: Not quantified. FDA describes these as harmful effects of chronic exposure to heavy metals in unapproved Ayurvedic drug products, and adds that large acute ingestions over short periods can be life-threatening
adverseEffects.note: Class-level. No adverse-effect report naming Kamsya Bhasma exists in the permitted sources, and the metal content of this preparation has not been measured in any permitted source.

adverseEffects.effect: Elevated blood lead, and in some people elevated blood mercury, among users of Ayurvedic preparations
adverseEffects.frequency: NCCIH cites a 2015 published survey of people who use Ayurvedic preparations in which 40 percent had elevated blood lead levels and some had elevated blood mercury levels, and a 2015 CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report case linking elevated blood lead in a 64-year-old woman to Ayurvedic preparations bought on the internet. NCCIH also states that arsenic poisoning from Ayurvedic products, although rare, can occur
adverseEffects.note: Class-level exposure data on Ayurvedic preparations generally. Not a report on this preparation, and neither the survey nor the case report identifies Kamsya Bhasma.

contraindications.condition: Children
contraindications.note: FDA states that adults and children can become very sick when heavy metals accumulate in their bodies over time. WHO states that lead can permanently affect children's brain development, reducing IQ and causing behavioural and learning problems, and that there is no level of lead exposure known to be without harmful effects. No paediatric data on this preparation exists in the permitted sources.

contraindications.condition: Kidney impairment or existing renal disease
contraindications.note: Kidney injury is one of the harmful effects FDA attributes to chronic heavy-metal accumulation, and WHO reports kidney effects from mercury ranging from increased urinary protein to kidney failure, with inorganic mercury salts inducing kidney toxicity if ingested. Renal impairment also reduces clearance of any absorbed metal. This is a hazard-specific entry, not a general precaution.

contraindications.condition: Known heavy-metal poisoning, elevated blood lead or mercury, or concurrent use of other bhasma, rasa shastra or metal-containing preparations
contraindications.note: Exposure is cumulative. Mikulski et al. found that a substantial share of positive samples exceeded acceptable daily intake for lead, mercury or arsenic on their own, before any second product is added, and NCCIH documents users of Ayurvedic preparations presenting with elevated blood lead. Because Kamsya Bhasma's own metal content is unmeasured, its contribution to total body burden cannot be estimated.

contraindications.condition: Any batch with no elemental analysis and no label declaration of metal content
contraindications.note: Bhalla and Pannu found that only 27.9% of the preparations they collected declared heavy metals on the label while metals were widespread in them, and FDA states there are no FDA-approved Ayurvedic products. An undeclared, unanalysed batch gives no basis on which exposure can be judged.

contraindications.condition: People who avoid animal-derived materials on religious, dietary or ethical grounds
contraindications.note: Liu et al. state that bhasma manufacture involves repeated incineration with herbal juice or decoction and animal-based products. No permitted source describes the manufacturing method of Kamsya Bhasma specifically, so whether animal-derived material is used in it is unknown and should be established from the manufacturer before use.

pregnancy.note: Avoid. WHO states that there is no level of lead exposure known to be without harmful effects, that lead stored in bone is released into the blood during pregnancy and becomes a source of exposure to the developing fetus, and that lead exposure during pregnancy can cause reduced fetal growth and preterm birth; WHO further states that exposure to mercury, even in small amounts, may cause serious health problems and is a threat to the development of the child in utero and early in life. This preparation is a metallic or mineral bhasma whose metal content has never been measured in a permitted source, and Bhalla and Pannu found metals in every preparation they tested while only 27.9% declared them, so it cannot be assumed metal-free. NCCIH advises pregnant or nursing people to consult a health care provider because some Ayurvedic products may contain harmful constituents. With a developmental neurotoxicant plausibly present, no measured content and no pregnancy data of any kind on Kamsya Bhasma, the honest grading is avoid rather than caution.

lactation.note: Avoid. FDA states that if a mother has heavy metals in her body the metals may enter her breast milk and be passed onto the baby during breastfeeding. WHO states that mercury exposure, even in small amounts, is a threat to the development of the child in utero and early in life, and that lead permanently affects children's brain development with no exposure level known to be without harmful effects; the WHO lead and mercury fact sheets do not themselves address transfer into breast milk. No lactation data on Kamsya Bhasma exists in the permitted sources, and its metal content is unmeasured.

neelam-pishti.insufficientReason: No authoritative source specific to Neelam Pishti was located in the permitted source set. The searches below were run on 2026-09-11 and are reported with what they actually returned, so they can be re-run. PubMed via NCBI E-utilities esearch (db=pubmed), preparation-name terms, each returning Count 0: Neelam Pishti (PubMed translates this to "Neelam"[All Fields] AND "Pishti"[All Fields]), Neelam Bhasma, Nilam Pishti, Neela Pishti, sapphire pishti. Broader terms do return records, none of them about a sapphire or Neelam preparation: sapphire bhasma returns 2 records, PMID 35277158 (antimicrobial potential of four mica drugs) and PMID 24993885 (review of mica drug processing); corundum ayurvedic returns 4, PMID 30237685 (Kushtae Shangarf, a Unani preparation), PMID 27502540 (Kanakasava in a rat asthma model), PMID 24993885 (the same mica review) and PMID 22754071 (toxicological study of Chondrokola Rosh on rat liver function tests); gemstone bhasma returns 2, PMID 30952470 (Swarna Makshika Bhasma prepared by an alternative heating method) and PMID 16632893 (chemical characterization of bhasmas); pishti heavy metal returns 2, PMID 39615446 (Badarashma Pishti) and PMID 35813362 (Trinakantamani Amber Pishti), which are the two pishti papers cited in this record; Neelam ayurveda returns 4, PMID 35255269 (an undergraduate curriculum paper), PMID 34961687 (a dermatophytosis case report), PMID 29076426 (a Swertia chirata review) and PMID 22131715 (an Uttara Vasti study), none concerning a gem or mineral preparation. Note that PubMed expands both sapphire and corundum to aluminium oxide, so those two are not name searches at all. PMC full text (db=pmc): "Neelam Pishti" returns Count 0, with the quoted phrase reported as not found and the query falling back to neelam AND pishti. "Neelam Bhasma" returns exactly one record, PMC3331307 (PMID 22557671), AV Sharma, Gems and their medicinal values, Anc Sci Life 1989;9(1):26-27, whose PMC page states only that "The medicinal uses of nine major gems (Navrtna) are enumerated here" and carries the article as a page scan whose text could not be retrieved here. Nothing is taken from it, and an enumeration of medicinal uses would in any case be excluded from a safety record; it is listed only because it is the single permitted-host record that matches the name at all. A domain-restricted web search of pharmacopoeia.gov.in, ayush.gov.in, who.int, iris.who.int, nccih.nih.gov, medlineplus.gov, fda.gov, ods.od.nih.gov and mskcc.org for "Neelam Pishti" and "Neelam Bhasma" returned no monograph, formulary entry or safety page naming either preparation. On that evidence, no monograph, clinical trial, case report, elemental analysis, human or animal dose, or pharmacopoeial standard for Neelam Pishti was found in the permitted sources. Because no permitted source identifies what a product sold under this name actually contains, no composition is asserted here and none can be assumed. No doseLimits field is carried, because no human or animal dose for this preparation exists in these sources. Every statement in this record is therefore class-level, about gem- and mineral-derived Rasa Shastra preparations or about the metals themselves, and each is labelled scope class-level.

heavyMetals.text: No allowed source located identifies the specific mineral or gemstone base of Neelam Pishti, and no elemental analysis of this named preparation has been published in the permitted sources, so its metal content is undetermined here and no composition can be assumed for any product sold under this name. The evidence below is class-level and applies to gem- and mineral-derived Rasa Shastra preparations generally. Jagtap et al. (2024) is used here only for classification: it states that in Ayurveda "Rasa Shastra includes the fabrication of Bhasmas and Pishti" and that "A limited number of studies have been carried out using Ayurvedic preparations derived from gems or precious stones that were used traditionally." That paper characterised Badarashma Pishti (Lapis judaicus), not a sapphire preparation, and reported calcite, quartz and aragonite with Ca, Mg, O and Si by EDAX; although its methods list "identification of heavy metals", the abstract reports no heavy-metal result, so no metal statement is taken from it. Saper et al. (2008) measured metals by x-ray fluorescence in Ayurvedic medicines bought over the Internet: 193 of the 230 requested medicines were received and analysed, and the prevalence of products with detectable lead, mercury or arsenic was 20.7% (95% CI, 15.2%-27.1%). Neither origin nor a manufacturing claim discriminated: US-manufactured prevalence was 21.7% (95% CI, 14.6%-30.4%) against 19.5% (95% CI, 11.3%-30.1%) for Indian products (P = .86), and among the metal-containing products 95% were sold by US web sites and 75% claimed Good Manufacturing Practices. Rasa shastra products had a greater prevalence of metals than non-rasa shastra products (40.6% vs 17.1%; P = .007) and higher median concentrations of lead (11.5 microg/g vs 7.0 microg/g; P = .03) and mercury (20,800 microg/g vs 34.5 microg/g; P = .04). The authors state that "All metal-containing products exceeded 1 or more standards for acceptable daily intake of toxic metals." Saper et al. (2004) found that 14 (20%) of 70 Ayurvedic herbal medicine products bought in Boston-area South Asian stores (95% CI, 11%-31%) contained heavy metals: lead (n = 13; median 40 microg/g; range 5-37,000), mercury (n = 6; median 20,225 microg/g; range 28-104,000) and/or arsenic (n = 6; median 430 microg/g; range 37-8130). They conclude that "If taken as recommended by the manufacturers, each of these 14 could result in heavy metal intakes above published regulatory standards", that users "may be at risk for heavy metal toxicity", and that "testing of Ayurvedic HMPs for toxic heavy metals should be mandatory." Mikulski et al. (2017, epub 2018) analysed 252 samples of Ayurvedic products and herbal supplements collected during a public health lead-poisoning cluster investigation. Lead was detected in 164 samples (65.1%), median 4.9 mg/kg, range 0.46-43,200 mg/kg; mercury in 97 (38.5%), median 53.0 mg/kg, range 0.8-279,000 mg/kg; arsenic in 82 (32.5%), median 8.4 mg/kg, range 1.0-44,800 mg/kg. The exceedance figures are taken with the authors' own denominators: "Almost half of samples containing mercury, 36% of samples containing lead and 39% of samples containing arsenic had concentrations of those metals per pill that exceeded, up to several thousand times, the recommended daily intake values for pharmaceutical impurities", which in Table 2 is 59 of the 164 lead-containing samples (35.8%), 48 of the 97 mercury-containing samples (49.5%) and 32 of the 82 arsenic-containing samples (39.5%) exceeding the USP oral permissible daily exposure per pill for a 50 kg person, assuming a 500 mg pill and one pill per day. The same paper documents lot-to-lot variability within one product family: Indukantham tablets from the same provider ranged from 43 to 43,200 mg/kg lead and 13 to 950 mg/kg mercury. The authors state a limitation that bears directly on interpretation: "This study did not conduct metals speciation analysis of the Ayurvedic products", so the chemical species present, and therefore the bioavailability behind those concentrations, are not established. Hore et al. (2022) reported on 584 samples of health remedies collected by the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene during poisoning investigations and store surveys between 2010 and 2019, finding a significant association between blood lead levels and estimated cumulative daily lead exposures among adult users of rasa shastra Ayurvedic medications, and that average blood lead levels among adult rasa shastra users were significantly higher than levels among those using other types of non-Ayurvedic health remedies. FDA warns that "using unapproved ayurvedic products containing harmful levels of heavy metals may cause heavy metal poisoning" and names lead, mercury, arsenic, iron and zinc among the metals such products may contain. One apparent counterpoint at pishti class level does not transfer: Joshi et al. (2020) reported for Trinakantamani (Amber) Pishti that "All heavy metals in the samples were within the permissible limit." Three facts void any transfer of that reassurance to a marketed gem pishti. The three samples were prepared by the investigators themselves using the standard reference method rather than bought from the market, so the finding says nothing about market supply; Trinakantamani is amber, a fossilised resin whose chief elements the same paper found to be carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so it is not a metal-bearing gem or mineral; and it is a different preparation from the one this record concerns.

adverseEffects.effect: Heavy metal poisoning, reported for Ayurvedic metallic and mineral products generally and not for Neelam Pishti specifically
adverseEffects.frequency: Not quantified for this preparation. At class level, NCCIH cites "A 2015 published survey of people who use Ayurvedic preparations showed that 40 percent had elevated blood levels of lead and some had elevated blood levels of mercury", and reports of the supplements tested in that context that "About one in four of the supplements tested had high levels of lead and almost half of them had high levels of mercury."
adverseEffects.note: FDA states that "Adults and children can become very sick when heavy metals accumulate in their bodies over time, and large acute ingestions over short periods of time can be life-threatening", and that use of these products may result in "high blood pressure, kidney injury, fatigue, gastrointestinal distress and neurologic symptoms", including abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea, nausea and vomiting, and burning or tingling in the fingers and/or toes, weakness in limbs and dizziness. NCCIH states that "Some Ayurvedic preparations may contain lead, mercury, or arsenic in amounts that can be toxic." No case report attributing any of these to Neelam Pishti was found in the permitted sources.

adverseEffects.effect: Arsenic poisoning and arsenic-related cancer risk
adverseEffects.frequency: NCCIH states that "Although rare, Ayurvedic products may cause arsenic poisoning." No frequency for cancer risk is given by either source, and none exists for this preparation.
adverseEffects.note: FDA states that "Chronic exposures to arsenic may increase the risk of cancer." This is a delayed-onset harm that does not present as an acute poisoning syndrome, so absence of acute symptoms is not evidence of safe exposure. Arsenic was detected in 32.5% of the 252 samples analysed by Mikulski et al. and in 6 of the 70 products tested by Saper et al. (2004). Nothing here is specific to Neelam Pishti, whose arsenic content is undetermined.

adverseEffects.effect: Non-metal toxic contaminants found alongside metals in one FDA-tested ayurvedic product
adverseEffects.frequency: A single-product finding, not a prevalence estimate. It is recorded because it shows that contamination in this product class is not confined to metals.
adverseEffects.note: FDA tested Rheumacare Ayurvedic Proprietary Medicine purchased from NavaFresh.com and reports that "The testing found high levels of lead and mercury, as well as the presence of strychnine, brucine toxins and arsenic." This result applies to that product only. It is not a finding about Neelam Pishti and not a class prevalence figure.

contraindications.condition: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
contraindications.note: FDA states that "If a mother has heavy metals in her body, the metals may enter her breast milk and be passed onto the baby during breastfeeding." NCCIH advises that "If you're pregnant or nursing, be sure to consult your (or your child's) health care provider as some Ayurvedic products may contain products that could be harmful." Lead, mercury and arsenic are documented in this product class and are developmental toxicants for which no safe exposure level can be shown from the available evidence. No pregnancy or lactation data specific to Neelam Pishti exists in the permitted sources.

contraindications.condition: Use in children
contraindications.note: FDA states that "Adults and children can become very sick when heavy metals accumulate in their bodies over time, and large acute ingestions over short periods of time can be life-threatening." Saper et al. (2004) compared estimated daily metal ingestion for adults and for children against US Pharmacopeia and US Environmental Protection Agency standards and concluded that each of the 14 metal-containing products, if taken as the manufacturer recommends, could result in intakes above published regulatory standards. No paediatric data specific to Neelam Pishti exists in the permitted sources.

contraindications.condition: Existing kidney disease or impaired renal function, and hypertension
contraindications.note: FDA names kidney injury and high blood pressure directly among the effects of heavy metal accumulation from unapproved ayurvedic products. Because the metal content of any product sold as Neelam Pishti is undetermined and the class is documented to carry lead, mercury and arsenic, a person with reduced renal clearance or established hypertension carries the class hazard at higher consequence. This is derived from class-level evidence and is not a finding about Neelam Pishti.

contraindications.condition: Known elevated blood lead, mercury or arsenic level, or any other ongoing source of exposure to these metals
contraindications.note: Hore et al. (2022) found a significant association between blood lead levels and estimated cumulative daily lead exposures among adult users of rasa shastra Ayurvedic medications, which is a dose-additive relationship: an additional source adds to an existing body burden rather than acting independently. Mikulski et al. document that the same product from the same provider can vary from 43 to 43,200 mg/kg lead, so an individual product cannot be assumed to be the low end of that range. This is derived from class-level evidence and is not a finding about Neelam Pishti.

pregnancy.note: No pregnancy data for Neelam Pishti exists in the permitted sources, and no permitted source establishes what a product sold under this name contains. The avoid grading, rather than caution, rests on class-level evidence: FDA warns that unapproved ayurvedic products may contain harmful levels of lead, mercury and arsenic; NCCIH advises consulting a health care provider during pregnancy because some Ayurvedic products may contain constituents that could be harmful; and Saper et al. (2008) documented that rasa shastra preparations carry a significantly higher prevalence of toxic metals (40.6% vs 17.1%; P = .007) and higher median lead and mercury concentrations than non-rasa shastra preparations. Lead, mercury and arsenic are developmental neurotoxicants for which no safe exposure level in pregnancy can be shown from the available evidence, and undetermined metal content in a product class documented to carry them is not a basis for a permissive grading.

lactation.note: No lactation data for Neelam Pishti exists in the permitted sources. FDA states directly that "If a mother has heavy metals in her body, the metals may enter her breast milk and be passed onto the baby during breastfeeding", and NCCIH advises consulting a health care provider while nursing because some Ayurvedic products may contain constituents that could be harmful. Transfer in milk means maternal intake becomes infant exposure, and the infant is exposed at the developmental stage at which lead and mercury neurotoxicity is most consequential, so avoid rather than caution is the supportable grading for a preparation of undetermined metal content within this class.

bhanga.evidenceSearch: Searches run 2026-09-11, reported so they can be re-run. (1) PubMed E-utilities esearch, db=pubmed, term 'Bhanga': 7 records (PMIDs 42250168, 40895842, 31831967, 26980601, 4460655, 29010075, 29009963); of these, only PMID 31831967 concerns Cannabis sativa, the others being a Dhaka-Bhanga expressway soil study, a Bangladesh buffalo review, a Bangladesh arsenite-oxidase soil study, a 1974 Bhanga tick virus isolation, and two 1931 Indian Medical Gazette case papers. (2) db=pubmed, term 'Bhanga AND cannabis': 1 record (31831967). (3) db=pubmed, term 'Shodhita Bhanga': 1 record (31831967). (4) db=pubmed, term 'Jalaprakshalana': 1 record (31831967). (5) db=pubmed, term 'Bhanga AND Ayurveda': 1 record (31831967). (6) PMC full-text esearch, db=pmc, term '"Shodhita Bhanga"': 1 record (PMC6891996, the full text of PMID 31831967). (7) db=pmc, term '"Bhanga" AND "Cannabis sativa"': 27 records; their titles were read and, apart from PMC6891996, none is a clinical or toxicological study of the Ayurvedic Bhanga preparation (they are ethnobotanical surveys, cannabis phytochemistry and general cannabis reviews, Ayurvedic formulation papers on other drugs, and historical articles). Full texts of the other 26 were not read, so this is a title-level statement. (8) A separate PMC record with a Bhanga entry, PMC4535066, does not appear in search (7) because it spells the drug 'Bhanga' with diacritics and misspells the binomial 'Cannabis seativa'; it was reached from a search for 'Shodhana Cannabis sativa water wash'. (9) Pharmacopoeial text: pharmacopoeia.gov.in and www.pharmacopoeia.gov.in did not resolve from this session (DNS NXDOMAIN, curl exit code 6), so the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India monograph for Bhanga could not be read directly and is reported here only as quoted by PMC6891996. (10) Ministry of Ayush documents: https://ayush.gov.in/resources/pdf/quality_standards/Drugs-and-Cosmetics-Act-Rules.pdf returned HTTP 404 and https://www.ayush.gov.in/docs/guideline_safety_toxicity.pdf returned HTTP 403, so no claim about Schedule E(1), Rule 161(2) or prescription-only status is made here. Conclusion: one permitted source (PMC6891996) reports a clinical study of a named Bhanga preparation and one (PMC4535066) gives a Bhanga entry of classical attributions; statements drawn from them are scoped preparation-specific, and everything drawn from the four general cannabis sources is scoped class-level. No elemental analysis, no pharmacovigilance case report and no pharmacopoeial monograph text for Bhanga was retrievable on a permitted host.

sources.title: Tavhare SD, Acharya R, Reddy RG, Dhiman KS. Management of chronic pain with Jalaprakshalana (water-wash) Shodhita (processed) Bhanga (Cannabis sativa L.) in cancer patients with deprived quality of life: An open-label single arm clinical trial. Ayu. 2019 Jan-Mar;40(1):34-43. PMCID PMC6891996, PMID 31831967, doi:10.4103/ayu.AYU_43_19
sources.tier: The only source located on a permitted host that reports a clinical study of a named Bhanga preparation, so statements drawn from it are scoped preparation-specific. Its limitations, carried on every statement taken from it: open-label, single-arm, no control group and no blinding; purposive (non-random) sampling at a single centre (RRA Podar Central Ayurveda Research Institute for Cancer, Mumbai); planned sample 40, 37 enrolled and 24 (64.86%) completed, 13 (35.14%) dropped out; treatment duration only 4 weeks with one further follow-up week for withdrawal assessment; adults 18-70 with cancer only; pre- and post-treatment laboratory investigations and ECG are described in the methods as done 'to check the safety aspects', but the article reports no laboratory or ECG results in any of its eleven tables or in its text. The article also carries efficacy material (pain, anxiety, depression, quality-of-life and performance-status outcomes); none of it is used in this record, which makes no efficacy or indication claim. This trial studied one specific Shodhana method, Jalaprakshalana (water-wash); it is not evidence about Bhanga processed by other methods or about unprocessed Bhanga.

sources.title: Maurya SK, Seth A, Laloo D, et al. Sodhana: An Ayurvedic process for detoxification and modification of therapeutic activities of poisonous medicinal plants. Anc Sci Life. 2015 Apr-Jun;34(4):188-197. PMCID PMC4535066, doi:10.4103/0257-7941.160862
sources.tier: A narrative review with a dedicated Bhanga entry, so the Bhanga statements taken from it are scoped preparation-specific. Its limitation, carried on every statement taken from it: the Bhanga entry reports classical and ethnopharmacological attributions with literature citations only. The review presents no chemical analysis, no animal study and no clinical data for Bhanga, and reports no measurement of what its named Shodhana media remove. Its general concluding sentence that 'Studies have shown that the toxic constituents are transferred into media rendering the drug nontoxic' is not tied by the review to Bhanga and is not carried here as a Bhanga finding. The review's list of traditional therapeutic uses for Bhanga is efficacy material and is not used in this record.

sources.title: Cannabis (Marijuana) and Cannabinoids: What You Need To Know, NCCIH
sources.tier: NCCIH. Addresses cannabis and cannabinoid products in general, not the Ayurvedic preparation Bhanga; every statement drawn from it is therefore scoped class-level. The page also carries efficacy material on pain, multiple sclerosis, chemotherapy-induced nausea, PTSD and sleep; none of it is used here.
